Support the reproduction claim with empirical evidence from the paper: (a) singleshot pruning experiments show a droparound $\rho\approx 0.01$ for multiple pruning methods on the Circle classification benchmark and consistent behavior across different network depths and widths (reported in the singleshot results and visualized in Figure 3 and supplementary figures); (b) multishot experiments reproduce method rankings and relative improvements observed in image experiments, such as SYNFLOW and MAGNITUDE being competitive for weak-ticket discovery when allowed iterative training (reported in Figure 4 and discussions comparing to VGG/ResNet behavior).
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Highlight the advantage of planted tickets for verifiability: because the planted-ticket design explicitly embeds a ground-truth sparse subnetwork with known sparsity $\rho$ and known performance, experiments can distinguish whether poor pruning outcomes are due to nonexistence of a ticket (fundamental limitation) or due to algorithmic failure; the planted benchmarks therefore provide verifiable baselines rather than only relative method comparisons.

Describe the practical artifacts that make the planted benchmarks realistic: the planted tickets are constructed to reflect common modeling challenges (radial symmetry, univariate piecewise-linear functions, and manifold regression), the experimental pipelines include noise levels and training protocols comparable to real tasks, and the authors reproduce VGG16 CIFAR10 behavior using planted tickets to demonstrate cross-domain relevance (see the VGG experiments and Figure 5).
Fig. 5

Take as given the experimental findings about singleshot failures (conclusion 4) and EDGE-POPUP's practical limitations even with annealing and extensions (conclusion 6); these upstream conclusions are treated as known starting points for the final empirical interpretation regarding algorithmic versus fundamental limitations.

Describe the specific VGG16-via-planting experiment used to probe algorithmic limitations: the authors used SYNFLOW to discover a weak ticket of sparsity $\rho=0.01$ from VGG16 via multishot pruning, trained that weak ticket to obtain its weights (i.e., a trained weak ticket), and then planted this trained weak ticket back into the randomly initialized VGG16 host network using the planting algorithm so that the host provably contains a strong ticket at sparsity $\rho=0.01$ (by construction).
Fig. 5

State the outcome when EDGE-POPUP was applied to the planted VGG16: running EDGE-POPUP (extended to score biases) on the network that provably contains the planted $\rho=0.01$ strong ticket failed to retrieve that planted strong ticket; EDGE-POPUP did not find a subnetwork at $\rho=0.01$ matching the planted baseline performance, as reported in the right panel of the authors' VGG16 experiment figure.
Fig. 5

Present the logical inference the authors draw from this controlled experiment: because the planted strong ticket of sparsity $\rho=0.01$ is known to exist inside the host network by construction (the planting procedure explicitly embedded it), the inability of EDGE-POPUP to find it cannot be attributed to nonexistence of such sparse strong tickets in random networks; rather, the failure indicates algorithmic limitations of current pruning methods (here exemplified by EDGE-POPUP) in locating extremely sparse strong tickets in practice.

Emphasize that this conclusion is empirical and conditional: the authors phrase this as an empirical conclusion drawn from the planted-ticket experiment on a realistic CNN setting (VGG16), supporting the view that current limitations in ticket sparsity are likely algorithmic; they note that the planting framework enables such experiments that separate algorithmic failure from fundamental nonexistence.

Treat the planting algorithm (conclusion 2) as implemented and state the reproducibility goal: the authors provide an implementation to enable reproduction of the planting procedure, data generation for the ReLU/Circle/Helix benchmarks, and the experimental protocols used in their pruning evaluations.

List the specific artifacts released and their scope: the released package contains (a) a reproducible implementation of the planting algorithm (the layerwise matching and per-neuron rescaling procedure), (b) synthetic benchmark data generators for the ReLU, Circle, and Helix tasks, (c) code implementing the experimental protocols including singleshot and multishot pruning routines, artificial-neural-network (ANN) hyperparameters, and an implementation of EDGE-POPUP extended to handle bias parameters, and (d) the scripts used to run the pruning evaluations reported in the paper.

Give the public release pointer the authors provide: the code and artifacts are made publicly available at the URL provided by the authors for reproducibility. The paper explicitly lists the release URL as "https://github.com/RelationalML/PlantNSeek/releases/tag/v1.0-beta" in a footnote in the experiments section, which serves as the access point for the implementation and supplementary material.
https://github.com/RelationalML/PlantNSeek/releases/tag/v1.0-beta

Note experimental details included to enable reuse: the released code includes data generation parameters (e.g., sample sizes, noise levels), network architecture builders for planted tickets, training hyperparameters (optimizer choices and learning rates such as Adam with learning rate 0.001 for pruning experiments), and pruning protocol details (number of rounds, annealing schedules) as described in the paper's experimental supplement, thereby supporting exact reproduction of the reported experiments.

open_questions.content: The authors explicitly identify multiple unresolved scientific issues for future work: (1) How can pruning algorithms for weak tickets be improved to discover tickets achieving the best possible sparsity (closing the gap between discovered and planted sparsities)? (2) How can one find weak tickets of high sparsity that match the performance of the full (mother) network without relying on intermediate training rounds (i.e., in a singleshot fashion)? (3) How can highly sparse strong lottery tickets be discovered algorithmically (improving methods like EDGE-POPUP to reliably locate planted strong tickets at extreme sparsities across realistic CNNs)? Additionally, the phenomenon of layer collapse and the markedly greater difficulty of regression and manifold-learning tasks compared to classification remain open targets: algorithmic strategies that prevent layer collapse without imposing unrealistic per-layer sparsity constraints, and scoring/pruning designs that are robust for regression/manifold representations, are left as open problems.
